title: Coral and Tin-Tin Save the Swan
markdown:
The rain had just stopped — pitter-patter-splish-splash rain, the kind that makes everything smell of damp soil and tiny busy earthworms stretching their legs. Garden patches were soggy and sparkling, as if someone had sprinkled a million tiny diamonds. The air was cool and fresh, a giant sigh after a big sneeze.

Coral the rabbit lived in a cozy burrow nestled by the most delicious-looking carrot patch, so sweet and plump the carrots practically winked. She had the fluffiest, bounciest tail you ever did see, a dandelion puffball ready to float. Her nose twitched a mile a minute, especially when she thought about gardening, which was, like, always. She dreamed of prize-winning pumpkins and roses so red they’d blush.

Her bestest friend in the whole wide world was not another fluffy rabbit, not a chatty squirrel. It was Tin-Tin. He wasn’t fluffy at all. He was a robot: shiny, clanky, positively delightful, a tin can that could walk and beep and boop. Big bright blue eyes lit up like little starry skies. When he walked, his metal feet went whirr-clank, whirr-clank, a cheerful rhythmic song of friendship. Need the ripest berries just out of reach? Tin-Tin. A watering can almost as tall as Coral? Tin-Tin. Although he sometimes got a little wobbly — bonk, a gentle nudge against a fence post, or thump, a soft landing near a pile of leaves — he always bounced back up, ready for more.

They were just about to head out to admire the newly washed rose bushes — extra pink and velvety after the rain — when they saw something truly alarming.

Mrs. Higgins had the most wonderful garden patch, the kind that won prizes for tall sunflowers and tomatoes as red as a firetruck. She had made something extra special for the Summer Fair’s Most Wonderful Thing prize. And guess what it was made of? Ice. A whole sculpture, shimmering and sparkling, carved into the most beautiful swan you ever did see. She had worked for days, brow furrowed, a little smile on her lips.

But the clouds parted like a curtain. The sun, which had been hiding, sent warm rays down. The swan began a very sad, very fast melt. Drip, drip. Crisp edges softened. The elegant neck went wobbly, jelly trying to stand.

Therefore Coral’s nose twitched faster than a hummingbird choosing a flower. “Tin-Tin. The swan is melting like a forgotten ice lolly. We have to do something.”

Tin-Tin’s eyes flashed. Beep-boop. Whirr-clank. Ice, his blinks suggested. Sun. Almost fire.

Coral hopped from foot to foot. “We need to cover it. Keep it cool. Mr. Gable’s shed. That giant thick cloth he uses for… picnics for giants? Big. Cool.”

Whizz went Tin-Tin. Adventure officially on.

So off they went. Hop-hop-whirrrr. They zoomed across the garden patches, past rows of sleepy cabbages and proud carrots. But it was a bit slippery from all that rain. A long wiggly earthworm slithered right across their path, looking quite pleased with its journey. Coral almost tripped, fluffy feet sliding on the damp soil. Therefore Tin-Tin, with a quick clank, stuck out a strong metal arm to steady her. “Whoa there, little earth-mover,” he beeped in his cheerful robot voice. Coral giggled, a happy little sound in the quiet patches.

Next they came to the Great Dandelion Patch, absolutely full of fluffy white heads like tiny fairy crowns, ready to be blown by the slightest puff. “Phew. Like running through a giant, tickly marshmallow cloud.” But a playful gust swept through. Therefore poof — dandelions flew everywhere, swirling and dancing, a fluffy snowstorm in the middle of summer. Quite a funny sight. Coral couldn’t help laughing, little white fluffies stuck in her fur.

Tin-Tin’s gears whirred with all his might, metal legs pumping. Clankety-clank-clank. But a rogue potato had clearly decided to go on a grand adventure, rolling right out of its neat row. Therefore his foot caught. “Whoopsie-daisy,” and a funny clanky little tumble. Robots are made of tough stuff. He bounced right back up, boing, like a super-springy toy.

Finally, after the tricky potato and the flying dandelions, they reached Mr. Gable’s shed. Painted a cheerful sky blue, the colour of a perfect summer day, but the door was a little stiff, probably from all that rain. Coral pushed with all her might, little bunny muscles straining. Tin-Tin, with a determined series of beeps that sounded like grunts, gave it a good clunk with his shiny head. “Open sesame… I mean, shed door,” Coral shouted, full of hope.

The door creaked open, a long drawn-out creeeeak. Inside it smelled of old wood, dry leaves, and something like a proper cozy shed. And there it was: a huge, thick, grey cloth, folded neatly. It looked as if it could wrap up a small elephant, or perhaps a very large picnic. Exactly what they needed.

“Yes,” Coral cheered, whiskers quivering. “Tin-Tin, can you help me carry it? It looks a bit heavy.”

Tin-Tin’s blue eyes glowed. “Beep-boop-yes. We can do it.”

It was heavy. Coral nudged it with her nose, trying to get it to slide, and Tin-Tin pushed with his strong robot hands, gears humming. A slow, steady trudge-trudge back across the garden patches. They didn’t stop, not for a second. They thought about Mrs. Higgins’s sad melting swan, and how much it meant to her. They knew it was important to keep it from disappearing into a watery puddle.

When they finally got back, the situation was quite dire. The swan’s proud wings drooped. It looked more like a shapeless blob with a beak than the majestic bird it had been. Drip, drip, splash. The ice was melting fast.

Therefore they worked together like a well-oiled — or rather, well-clanked — machine. Coral nudged the thick cloth with her nose, wrangling it into place, while Tin-Tin, with a mighty heave of metal arms, draped the big cool fabric over the top, tucking and smoothing so no sneaky sunbeams could get through. Whoosh went the cloth, a cozy protective blanket.

They stood back, panting a little, hearts thumping with exhaustion and hope. The drip had slowed to a tiny drip… drip… like a shy whisper.

Coral scanned the scene. The sun was still shining, but it felt different. On one side of the shed, where the sun hit directly, it felt warm and cozy. Under the grey cloth it felt much cooler, like a shady spot under a tall tree. “Look, Tin-Tin. Warm over there. Not melting so fast here. The cloth is a big shade-maker.”

Tin-Tin beeped happily, cheerful triumphant noises. Whirr-clank-yay. He understood. The sun’s warmth wanted to give the ice swan a big warm hug. The cloth was a friendly bodyguard: not today, sunshine.

Just then Mrs. Higgins came bustling in, face etched with worry. “Oh dear, my beautiful swan. It’s—” She stopped, mouth falling open. The melting had almost, almost stopped. Her swan was still there, a little wobbly, mostly, gloriously safe.

“Oh, Coral. Tin-Tin. You saved it. You wonderful, clever, amazing things.” She gave Coral a gentle pat and Tin-Tin a little polish on his shiny arm. “However did you do it?”

Coral puffed out her chest. “We got Mr. Gable’s super cool cloth.”

Mrs. Higgins laughed, a warm tinkling sound. “My hero rabbits and robots. You both deserve a treat. I just baked some of my famous carrot cakes, still warm from the oven.”

And so they sat together under sunshine that wasn’t quite so scorchingly hot, munching delicious crumbly carrot cake. The ice swan stood in the centre of the patch, a little droopy, safe and sound. Tin-Tin’s eyes reflected a last slow drip that had decided to be still.

Munch, munch, whirr. The cloth held. The neck held. The afternoon, against all meteorological advice, held too.
